---
title: "Distance and scaling"
execute:
  cache: false
---

The [Peterson-Barney table introduced on the preceding page](representing-objects.qmd) gives F1 and F2 in hertz. A distance calculation must state how those two measurements become one comparison. Here we compare raw hertz, global standardization, and a speaker-relative representation before fixing the geometry used on later pages.

## Loading the rows and constructing three geometries

```{r}
source_environment <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
utils::data("pb52", package = "phonTools", envir = source_environment)
pb52 <- source_environment$pb52

expected_columns <- c(
  "type", "sex", "speaker", "vowel", "repetition",
  "f0", "f1", "f2", "f3"
)
stopifnot(
  identical(dim(pb52), c(1520L, 9L)),
  identical(names(pb52), expected_columns),
  all(table(pb52$speaker) == 20L)
)

speaker_labels <- c(c = "Children", m = "Men", w = "Women")
vowels <- pb52 |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    row_id = dplyr::row_number(),
    token_id = sprintf(
      "speaker-%02d-%s-repetition-%d", speaker, vowel, repetition
    ),
    speaker_type = factor(
      speaker_labels[as.character(type)],
      levels = c("Men", "Women", "Children")
    ),
    global_z_f1 = as.numeric(scale(f1)),
    global_z_f2 = as.numeric(scale(f2))
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(speaker) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    z_f1 = (f1 - mean(f1)) / stats::sd(f1),
    z_f2 = (f2 - mean(f2)) / stats::sd(f2)
  ) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()

representations <- list(
  raw_hz = as.matrix(vowels[, c("f1", "f2")]),
  global_z = as.matrix(vowels[, c("global_z_f1", "global_z_f2")]),
  within_speaker_z = as.matrix(vowels[, c("z_f1", "z_f2")])
)

speaker_check <- vowels |>
  dplyr::group_by(speaker) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    mean_z_f1 = mean(z_f1),
    mean_z_f2 = mean(z_f2),
    sd_z_f1 = stats::sd(z_f1),
    sd_z_f2 = stats::sd(z_f2),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

stopifnot(
  max(abs(speaker_check$mean_z_f1)) < 1e-12,
  max(abs(speaker_check$mean_z_f2)) < 1e-12,
  max(abs(speaker_check$sd_z_f1 - 1)) < 1e-12,
  max(abs(speaker_check$sd_z_f2 - 1)) < 1e-12
)
```

## Three coordinate systems

The same F1-F2 token can occupy three coordinate systems:

| Representation | Coordinate | Substantive commitment |
|---|---|---|
| Raw hertz | \(F_{ij}\) | A one-hertz difference has the same numerical meaning across speakers, and features with larger hertz spreads contribute more. |
| Global standardization | \((F_{ij}-\bar F_j)/s_j\) | The complete sample supplies one shared origin and unit for each formant. |
| Within-speaker standardization | \((F_{isj}-\bar F_{sj})/s_{sj}\) | A token is located relative to the complete observed vowel space of its own speaker. |

To make the change concrete, consider the first *heed* and *hid* productions by
speaker 1. Their observed coordinates and distances are computed from the rows
above.

```{r}
hand_rows <- c(1L, 3L)
hand_coordinates <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(
  names(representations),
  function(name) {
    coordinates <- representations[[name]][hand_rows, , drop = FALSE]
    data.frame(
      representation = name,
      token = vowels$token_id[hand_rows],
      coordinate_1 = coordinates[, 1],
      coordinate_2 = coordinates[, 2],
      distance = c(
        sqrt(sum((coordinates[1, ] - coordinates[2, ])^2)),
        NA_real_
      )
    )
  }
))
knitr::kable(hand_coordinates, digits = 3)
```

For each representation, the displayed distance is

$$
\sqrt{(x_{11}-x_{21})^2+(x_{12}-x_{22})^2}.
$$

The arithmetic is unchanged across rows of the table; only the coordinates
supplied to it change. Raw hertz preserves between-speaker anatomy and recording
scale. Global standardization equalizes the two sample-wide formant spreads but
retains between-speaker shifts. Within-speaker standardization removes each
speaker's observed location and scale, which may reduce anatomy-related
differences but can also remove stable sociolinguistic variation. We use the last
geometry because our comparison concerns relative locations within an
observed speaker's vowel space.

## Euclidean distance

For two rows $\mathbf{x}_i$ and $\mathbf{x}_{i'}$ with $p$ features, [**Euclidean distance**](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14) is

$$
d(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_{i'})
=
\sqrt{
\sum_{m=1}^{p}
(x_{im}-x_{i'm})^2
}.
$$

Subtracting within columns keeps the comparison feature-specific. Squaring makes positive and negative differences contribute in the same direction, and adding gives an axis-aligned geometry. The units of that geometry come from the feature transformation.

For the main representation, we standardize within speaker:

$$
z_{isj}
=
\frac{F_{isj}-\bar F_{sj}}{s_{sj}},
\qquad j\in\{1,2\},
$$

where $\bar F_{sj}$ and $s_{sj}$ are the mean and [sample standard deviation](../random-variables-and-distributions/standard-deviation.qmd) across speaker $s$'s `r unique(as.integer(table(vowels$speaker)))` tokens. The standard deviation supplies the typical root-mean-squared distance from that speaker's mean on formant $j$. Distance becomes

$$
d(i,i')
=
\sqrt{
(z_{i1}-z_{i'1})^2+(z_{i2}-z_{i'2})^2
}.
$$

The transformation asks about relative position inside each observed speaker's
vowel space, so we use it for the comparisons that follow. This choice removes
stable between-speaker location and scale along with anatomy-related variation.
Peterson and Barney did not use this preprocessing step in the historical study.

## One observed token under three scales

We select the observed token nearest the center of the speaker-relative representation, then find its nearest other token independently in each geometry. Intended vowel and speaker type enter only after the neighbors have been found.

```{r}
pairwise_squared_distance <- function(x, centers) {
  x2 <- rowSums(x^2)
  c2 <- rowSums(centers^2)
  pmax(outer(x2, c2, "+") - 2 * tcrossprod(x, centers), 0)
}

reference_row <- which.min(rowSums(
  sweep(
    representations$within_speaker_z,
    2,
    colMeans(representations$within_speaker_z),
    "-"
  )^2
))

nearest_neighbor <- lapply(representations, function(x) {
  squared <- pairwise_squared_distance(x, x)
  diag(squared) <- Inf
  max.col(-squared, ties.method = "first")
})

distance_reference <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(
  names(representations),
  function(name) {
    neighbor <- nearest_neighbor[[name]][reference_row]
    data.frame(
      representation = name,
      reference_row = reference_row,
      reference_token = vowels$token_id[reference_row],
      neighbor_row = neighbor,
      neighbor_token = vowels$token_id[neighbor],
      distance = sqrt(sum(
        (representations[[name]][reference_row, ] -
           representations[[name]][neighbor, ])^2
      )),
      same_intended_vowel =
        vowels$vowel[reference_row] == vowels$vowel[neighbor]
    )
  }
))

knitr::kable(distance_reference, digits = 4)
```

The reference row is `r reference_row`. Its nearest observed neighbor changes from row `r distance_reference$neighbor_row[distance_reference$representation == "raw_hz"]` in raw hertz to row `r distance_reference$neighbor_row[distance_reference$representation == "within_speaker_z"]` after within-speaker standardization. Scaling has changed the neighborhood without changing a token's measurements.

## Comparing the induced neighborhoods

```{r}
distance_summary <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(
  names(representations),
  function(name) {
    nearest <- nearest_neighbor[[name]]
    data.frame(
      representation = name,
      same_vowel_rate = mean(vowels$vowel == vowels$vowel[nearest]),
      same_speaker_type_rate = mean(vowels$type == vowels$type[nearest])
    )
  }
))

knitr::kable(distance_summary, digits = 3)
```

Under raw hertz, `r scales::percent(distance_summary$same_vowel_rate[distance_summary$representation == "raw_hz"], accuracy = 0.1)` of nearest neighbors share intended-vowel metadata and `r scales::percent(distance_summary$same_speaker_type_rate[distance_summary$representation == "raw_hz"], accuracy = 0.1)` share speaker type. In the within-speaker geometry, those rates are `r scales::percent(distance_summary$same_vowel_rate[distance_summary$representation == "within_speaker_z"], accuracy = 0.1)` and `r scales::percent(distance_summary$same_speaker_type_rate[distance_summary$representation == "within_speaker_z"], accuracy = 0.1)`, respectively. This post hoc comparison suggests that the speaker-relative geometry reduces a salient speaker-type organization while increasing alignment with the elicitation labels.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8.2
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| fig-alt: "Within-speaker standardized F2 by F1 measurements for Peterson and Barney tokens, separated into panels for men, women, and children."

ggplot2::ggplot(vowels, ggplot2::aes(x = z_f2, y = z_f1)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(color = "grey25", alpha = 0.28, size = 0.7) + # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~speaker_type, nrow = 1) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_reverse() +
  ggplot2::scale_y_reverse() +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Within-speaker standardized F2",
    y = "Within-speaker standardized F1"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_classic(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(
    strip.background = ggplot2::element_blank(),
    strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "plain")
  )
```

## The prediction information set

Within-speaker standardization uses a speaker's complete unlabeled 20-token panel to determine that speaker's mean and standard deviation. The later speaker-blocked analyses thus target a new speaker whose complete calibration panel is available. No held-out token estimates a centroid or mixture component, but held-out measurements do determine their speaker's coordinate system.

This distinction follows the [prediction information set](../model-criticism-and-prediction/prediction-targets.qmd#the-prediction-information-set). The analysis does not predict one isolated token from a speaker with no calibration data. It also leaves dependence among the 20 transformed rows unmodeled.

This is the **calibration-panel target**: transfer to a new speaker whose complete,
unlabeled twenty-token panel is available to define that speaker's origin and
scale. A deployable first-token target would instead require a transformation
estimated without the rest of that speaker's panel, perhaps from training speakers
or from external anatomical information. The two targets supply different
information at prediction time.

## Scaling does not establish relevance

Standardization gives each chosen coordinate a comparable observed spread. It does not make F1 and F2 equally reliable, independent, or exhaustive. A duplicated feature would receive double influence, while an omitted dynamic or F3 measurement receives none.

Thus, Euclidean distance remains conditional on the representation. A high-quality clustering under this geometry may summarize recurring F1-F2 regions, but it cannot establish that this geometry captures every linguistically relevant relation.

## Checking the geometry

1. Which observed token is nearest to row `r reference_row` under each representation?
2. Why can the nearest neighbor change when the acoustic measurements do not?
3. What does one unit mean after within-speaker standardization?
4. Which information from a held-out speaker defines the validation coordinate system?
5. Why do post-fit intended-vowel matches not constitute label leakage?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The code table identifies the nearest row separately under each representation.
2. Scaling changes the coordinate differences that Euclidean distance squares and
   adds.
3. One unit is one within-speaker sample standard deviation for that formant.
4. All twenty unlabeled measurements define the held-out speaker's means and scales.
5. The labels are inspected only after distances have been constructed and neighbors
   selected.

</details>

## Recap

1. Distance is inseparable from the coordinate system supplied to it.
2. Within-speaker standardization targets relative vowel-space position and removes
   both anatomy-related and potentially meaningful stable variation.
3. Later validation concerns a complete calibration panel, not an isolated first
   token.

The [next page](k-means.qmd#assignments-centroids-and-loss) uses this declared
speaker-relative geometry to estimate centroids without intended-vowel labels.
